title: Proteome-scale prediction of molecular interactions and affinities

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a generalizable computational capability to predict which proteins interact with small molecules or other proteins, which pairs do not bind, where interacting partners contact one another, and how strongly they bind under specified conditions. Its intended scope includes unfamiliar protein families and molecular partners, as well as difficult disordered and membrane-associated targets. Proteome-scale coverage means making these predictions broadly enough, and at practical enough computational cost, to screen interactions across an organism’s protein repertoire. This is the proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Three distinct predictions must work together: whether binding occurs, the geometry of the bound complex, and binding affinity. A plausible predicted structure does not by itself establish a dependable affinity, and ranking affinities among known binders does not show that a model can distinguish binders from nonbinders. The supplied benchmark directly illustrates these distinctions for protein–ligand prediction; it does not evaluate the entire proposed range of partners and targets.

significance.text: If reliable generalization and practical computational costs were achieved, large interaction screens could help researchers prioritize which molecular pairs to test experimentally. The supplied study places protein–ligand affinity prediction within virtual screening, structure-based drug discovery and lead optimization. Extending dependable predictions across a proteome could make these workflows substantially more systematic, while still requiring experimental confirmation.

Conditional synthesis: dependable binding and nonbinding predictions could help identify candidate interaction partners and assess molecular selectivity across many proteins. Affinity estimates would add a quantitative basis for ranking those candidates, while interface predictions could guide experiments or molecular modifications. These benefits depend on coverage, uncertainty calibration and performance on unfamiliar inputs; the supplied benchmark does not demonstrate proteome-wide screening or its downstream benefits.

Impact boundary: molecular binding is only one component of biological function and drug performance. Even a successful interaction predictor would not by itself establish delivery to the relevant tissue or cellular compartment, safety, efficacy, or the consequences of an interaction in a living system. Computational screening could focus laboratory work, but the proposed innovation does not establish that most laboratory assays could be replaced.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in the supplied evidence is dependable affinity prediction under the structural-input conditions encountered in deployment, together with discrimination between binding and nonbinding pairs. In the evaluated workflows, prediction quality depended on how the complex structure was obtained, and averaging predictions across multiple poses did not restore near-crystal performance for perturbed inputs. Better structural plausibility therefore cannot simply be assumed to deliver reliable interaction energetics.

Generalization is a separate barrier. All evaluated complexes were confirmed binders, so the study could not establish whether the models assign appropriately weaker affinities to nonbinding pairs. All benchmark structures also predated the AlphaFold3 training cutoff, limiting conclusions about deployment on unfamiliar targets. A broader capability needs evidence that its performance survives changes in protein family, partner chemistry and structural-input quality, rather than relying on familiar benchmark distributions.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: extending the capability to specified environmental conditions, protein partners, disordered regions and membrane-associated targets requires representing the molecular states and contexts that determine binding. Flexible conformations and alternative interfaces complicate the relationship between a single predicted pose and an observed affinity. Models would also need useful uncertainty estimates when these states or contexts are poorly determined. These are barriers implied by the intended scope; their severity and current degree of resolution are not established by the supplied protein–ligand study.

Engineering synthesis: proteome-scale usefulness additionally requires manageable computational costs, consistent handling of heterogeneous inputs, and predictions that remain useful when most screened pairs may not bind. The supplied evidence does not establish the throughput, coverage or error rates necessary for that operating regime.

current_state.text: Eaves and Woldring’s “Robustness of Protein–Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction Models to Docked and Predicted Structures,” dated June 23, 2026, evaluated five reproducible protein–ligand affinity prediction pipelines. Their performance depended on structural input. AlphaFold3 co-folding was competitive with docking into apo receptors and significantly better for two of the five pipelines. This establishes a useful result within the evaluated workflows, rather than a general demonstration of interaction or affinity prediction.

Multipose averaging had effects that depended on the source of the structures and did not recover near-crystal performance for any perturbed input in the study. This result concerns the evaluated pipelines and the tested averaging approach. It does not establish that every affinity method fails on predicted or docked structures, nor that future methods cannot overcome this sensitivity.

The evaluation used confirmed protein–ligand binders throughout, leaving binding-versus-nonbinding discrimination untested. Its CASF-2016 structures all predated the AlphaFold3 training cutoff. The article consequently cautions that the reported co-folding performance may be optimistic relative to deployment on targets absent from AlphaFold3’s training data. Predating the cutoff does not itself establish that every evaluated structure was in the training data, but it limits the strength of claims about unfamiliar-target generalization.

The supplied review reports verification of the full main-article HTML without truncation or reported extraction problems. Supplementary material and figure images were not inspected, so interpretations here are bounded by the main-text findings recorded in that review. The supplied record identifies a dated journal article and DOI, rather than a preprint; the principal qualifications concern evaluation scope and generalization.

Evidence boundary: the supplied material does not establish the field-wide state as of November 2026. The review’s bounded freshness-search record was empty, leaving subsequent advances unverified. It also does not independently substantiate the earlier broad characterization of AlphaFold3 as a major advance across complex structure prediction, or determine present capability across protein partners, disordered targets and membrane-associated targets. Those limitations do not invalidate the reported June 2026 findings or show that unexamined results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: conduct prospective, blinded evaluations spanning diverse protein families, small molecules and protein partners. Measure binding-versus-nonbinding discrimination, binding geometry where experimentally measurable, and affinity prediction with calibrated uncertainty as separate outcomes. Include difficult targets, held-out families and chemistries, and explicit assessment of disordered and membrane-associated targets. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established community standards.
completion_criteria.label: Blinded prospective tests demonstrate discrimination, geometry and calibrated affinity prediction

completion_criteria.text: The benchmark directly motivates testing with structures representative of actual screening workflows: docking into apo or predicted receptors and co-folded predicted complexes. Evaluation should also include nonbinding pairs, addressing the study’s known-binder-only limitation. Performance on experimentally resolved complexes alone would leave these documented deployment questions unanswered.
completion_criteria.label: Screening evaluations include apo and predicted structures with nonbinding pairs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed assessment design: prespecify experimental conditions, operational definitions of binding and nonbinding, generalization splits, numerical success thresholds and uncertainty-calibration criteria. Compare performance with experimental uncertainty and relevant existing screening methods. Report results separately by target class and structural-input source so that aggregate performance does not conceal important failures. No numerical threshold is supplied here because the record does not establish an appropriate universal value.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified evaluation criteria support comparisons and stratified performance reporting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: provide sufficient methods, data and executable workflows for independent groups to repeat the evaluation, and seek confirmation on prospectively collected interactions. Report computational cost, throughput, coverage and failure rates at the intended screening scale. Successful finite tests would demonstrate breadth over the tested domains and conditions; they would not establish literal universality across every protein, partner or environment.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible workflows report screening-scale resource costs and practical limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BIF-02, “Predictive molecular dynamics from biological sequence,” has the closest overlap through molecular energetics and dynamics. BIF-09 retains a distinct goal: interaction screening and affinity prediction could be useful without general prediction of molecular trajectories or transition rates. Conversely, a dynamics capability would not automatically establish accurate binding-versus-nonbinding classification at screening scale.

Roster-based synthesis: BIF-06, “A general decoder for unknown gene and protein functions,” could use predicted interaction partners as evidence about function, but binding alone does not establish a protein’s biological role. BIF-07, “Computational reconstruction of organism-scale molecular maps,” overlaps through interaction maps, while also requiring broader spatial and organism-level organization. BIF-04, “General reconstruction of causal cellular networks,” requires causal relationships that cannot be inferred from molecular binding alone.

Roster-based synthesis: BIF-03, “A transferable, predictive virtual cell,” could incorporate interaction and affinity predictions as molecular inputs, but predicting whole-cell behavior requires additional capabilities. BIF-08, “Reliable reconstruction and forecasting of single-cell fates,” concerns changes in cellular state and developmental outcomes; interaction predictions could inform mechanisms without independently establishing those forecasts.

Roster-based synthesis: BIF-01, “A predictive decoder for the regulatory genome,” overlaps where proteins interact with regulatory machinery, but its central task is predicting regulatory effects from genomic information. BIF-05, “Computer-aided design of functional whole genomes,” and BIF-13, “Predictive design of functional genetic circuits and pathways,” could use interaction predictions to evaluate components and unintended interactions. Their design goals additionally require coordinated function beyond pairwise molecular binding.

Roster-based synthesis: BIF-10, “A broadly capable autonomous bioinformatics discovery system,” could use this capability within a larger discovery workflow; autonomy and broad scientific reasoning remain separate requirements. BIF-11, “Accessible, uncertainty-aware assembly of complex genomes,” addresses sequence reconstruction rather than molecular interaction prediction. BIF-12, “Strain-resolved discovery and functional profiling of microbial communities,” could draw on interaction predictions when interpreting microbial proteins, but also requires community composition, strain resolution and functional profiling.

unresolved_issues: Field-wide progress after the June 2026 study remains unverified; the supplied freshness-search record was empty.
The supplied evidence does not determine current capability across protein–protein partners, disordered targets, membrane-associated targets or varying environmental conditions.
Binding-versus-nonbinding discrimination remains unevaluated for the five benchmarked pipelines in the supplied study.
Performance on genuinely unfamiliar targets remains uncertain because all benchmark structures predated the AlphaFold3 training cutoff; actual training-set membership is not resolved here.
Numerical success thresholds, binding definitions, acceptable computational costs and required proteome coverage remain to be specified for the proposed demonstration.
Supplementary material and figure images were not inspected in the supplied review and could contain relevant details beyond its main-text account.

brief.title: Predicting which molecules bind across all proteins
possible: Researchers could screen an organism’s full set of proteins to predict which small molecules or other proteins bind to them, which pairs stay apart, where they touch and how strongly they bind under specified conditions. This would extend to unfamiliar partners and proteins that are flexible or sit in cell membranes.
why: Drug researchers could prioritize laboratory tests, compare how selectively a candidate binds across proteins and choose molecular changes to investigate. Biologists could identify candidate interaction partners and plan experiments around their predicted contact sites.

sources.who: Joelle N Eaves and Daniel R Woldring
sources.showed: Binding-strength predictions depended on how the molecular structures were generated. Averaging predictions across several possible arrangements failed to restore performance close to that obtained with experimentally measured structures.
sources.quote:
Multipose
averaging showed source-dependent effects and did not recover near-crystal
performance for any perturbed input.
sources.cited_for: Reliable binding-strength estimates require tests using the computed structures researchers would use in practice.
sources.not_established: The study tested known binding pairs, leaving rejection of nonbinding pairs and performance on unfamiliar targets unresolved.

sources.showed: Their preprint presents FlowDock, which jointly predicts bound structures and binding strength. It reported a 51% success rate for finding bound arrangements from proteins initially modeled without their partners.
sources.quote:
FlowDock provides predicted structural confidence
scores and binding affinity values with each of its generated protein-ligand complex structures
sources.cited_for: A single model can produce both molecular arrangements and binding-strength estimates.
sources.not_established: These benchmarks leave broad rejection of nonbinding pairs and dependable screening across an organism’s proteins unresolved.

sources.who: David Graber, Peter Stockinger, Fabian Meyer and collaborators
sources.showed: They created CleanSplit, training data filtered to remove similarities to test cases. Existing models lost accuracy after retraining, while their GEMS model retained strong performance on independent tests.
sources.quote:
Retraining current top-performing models on CleanSplit 
caused their benchmark performance to drop substantially, indicating 
that the performance of existing models is largely driven by data leakage.
sources.cited_for: Tests must control similarities between training and test examples to measure performance on unfamiliar molecular pairs.
sources.not_established: Independent benchmark accuracy leaves performance with computed structures and across the full range of protein targets unresolved.

sources.who: Andrew Savinov, Sebastian Swanson, Amy E Keating and Gene-Wei Li
sources.showed: FragFold predicted where protein fragments bind and inhibit target proteins. Experiments supported predicted contact arrangements, including previously unknown ones.
sources.quote: Across full protein sequences, 68% of FragFold-predicted binding peaks match experimentally measured inhibitory peaks.
sources.cited_for: Protein-fragment binding predictions can agree with experimental measurements of inhibition.
sources.not_established: Fragment inhibition results leave dependable binding-strength prediction across diverse molecular partners unresolved.

shown: Morehead and Cheng’s FlowDock combines structure and binding-strength prediction. Graber and colleagues’ GEMS retains accuracy after filtering similarities between training and test cases. Savinov and colleagues’ FragFold connects predicted fragment binding with measured inhibition.

Eaves and Woldring found that binding-strength accuracy depended on the source of the structures. Together, these results demonstrate parts of the capability in bounded tests. Dependable screening across an organism’s full protein set remains to be demonstrated.
missing: A system must reliably distinguish binding from nonbinding pairs while predicting contact sites and binding strength.
Performance must hold across unfamiliar protein families, molecular partners, flexible proteins and proteins in membranes.
Predictions need dependable uncertainty estimates under specified binding conditions and with computed structures.
Independent demonstrations must establish affordable computing costs, broad coverage and useful error rates at screening scale.

milestones.label: Blinded tests establish binding, contact sites and binding strength
milestones.explanation: Blinded tests on new pairs would have to measure binding, contact arrangements and binding strength, with uncertainty matching observed errors across diverse and difficult targets. This would establish breadth beyond familiar examples.

milestones.label: Screening tests succeed with computed structures and nonbinding pairs
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to include nonbinding pairs and structures computed from proteins without bound partners or predicted jointly with partners. This would establish performance with inputs used in practical screening.

milestones.label: Predefined criteria expose performance across target classes
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to set conditions, binding definitions, success thresholds and uncertainty criteria beforehand, then compare methods and report performance by target and input type. This would expose failures hidden by averages.

milestones.label: Independent groups reproduce results at practical screening costs
milestones.explanation: Independent groups would have to repeat the tests and confirm new interactions using shared workflows that report computing costs, speed, coverage and failures. This would establish reproducibility and practical screening limits.

uncertain: How much performance will fall on genuinely unfamiliar proteins and molecular partners remains unclear.
It remains unclear how reliably models can handle flexible molecular states and changing binding conditions.
Appropriate success thresholds, binding definitions, computing budgets and required protein coverage remain open.

page.title: Proteome-wide prediction of interactions and binding affinities
page.definition: Computational prediction of binding versus nonbinding, bound geometry and equilibrium affinity—the strength of binding—for protein pairs and protein–small-molecule pairs across a named organism’s complete protein repertoire. Predictions specify environmental conditions and extend to protein families and partners absent from training.

goal.need: HuRI illustrates the number of candidate pairs a proteome-wide predictor must handle. In CASP16, 28 groups submitted Stage 1 affinity predictions; assessment retained 122 targets after excluding previously disclosed data. The maximum sample-size-weighted Kendall rank correlation was 0.39, versus an estimated experimental-noise ceiling of 0.73 assuming threefold assay uncertainty. Joint predictions would prioritise experimental pairs and quantify binding strength.

figures.caption: Scale of the HuRI protein interaction screen, published on 8 April 2020.
figures.note: Verified interactions are detected positives; the remaining candidate pairs are not established nonbinders.

statements.quote: we would look for affinity methods to approach the theoretical maximum value of Kendall's τ
statements.context: The attainable rank correlation depends on experimental uncertainty and the distribution of measured affinities.

statements.quote: accelerate the development of computational approaches to small molecule hit-finding
This approach stands to enable proteome-wide discovery of inhibitory protein fragments
statements.context: Protein fragments are peptides taken from longer protein sequences.

completion.title: Independent experiments reproduce joint binding, structure and affinity predictions across a proteome.
completion.criterion: An independent laboratory repeats m4 using the same frozen workflow and new blinded experimental pairs. Predictions cover all protein pairs in the same reference proteome and every protein against the declared small-molecule library. Validation includes both partner classes, protein families absent from training, membrane proteins and disordered regions. All tested binding/nonbinding calls match experimentally determined status at stated assay detection limits; every structurally measured binder passes m1, and every binder with measured equilibrium affinity has absolute binding-free-energy error ≤1 kcal/mol under specified conditions.
completion.set_by: Atlas; a finite integrated demonstration and independent experimental replication.
completion.basis: Searches of CASP/CAPRI criteria, CACHE rules, HuRI verification criteria, DARPA/IARPA programmes and developer material found no combined proteome-wide passing test or aggregate error and computing budget. Known-binder and crystal-input benchmarks do not establish the joint capability. The 2026 evaluation guidelines were accessible only in abstract. Atlas therefore combines published component criteria for one named proteome with independent experimental replication.

milestones.title: A predicted complex has ligand RMSD <2 Å or protein-interface DockQ >0.23, according to partner class.
milestones.criterion: Against an experimental complex, a small-molecule pose has pocket-aligned heavy-atom RMSD <2 Å; a protein interface has DockQ >0.23, a dimensionless score combining contact recovery and coordinate deviations. These are per-complex criteria. FlowDock’s preprint, revised on 24 March 2025 and not peer reviewed, reported 51% success on 308 complexes at RMSD ≤2 Å plus PoseBusters validity. FragFold, published on 3 February 2025, obtained native-like contacts for 13/15 fragment–protein interactions using its own contact criteria; this is not a DockQ assessment.
milestones.set_by: Protein–ligand RMSD and protein-interface DockQ conventions, as applied by Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs in AlphaFold 3, Figure 1c; the thresholds are specific to the respective partner classes.
milestones.threshold_quote: percentage DockQ > 0.23 for protein–protein and protein–antibody interfaces.

milestones.title: A predicted interaction has two experimental supports, including a direct or binary binding assay.
milestones.criterion: A predicted interaction has ≥2 experimental supports, including a binary interaction or direct-binding assay. Small-molecule hits also undergo orthogonal binding confirmation and solubility and aggregation checks. CACHE #1, published on 5 November 2024, tested 1,955 initial molecules and confirmed seven chemical series in two orthogonal assays, with affinities of 18–140 µM. HuRI supplies experimentally verified protein reference pairs; its construction does not evaluate computational predictions.
milestones.set_by: HuRI consortium, Lit-BM reference-set definition, for protein interactions; CACHE Challenge #1 organisers, experimental hit-confirmation protocol, for small molecules.
milestones.threshold_quote: each having ≥2 pieces of experimental evidence, with at least one from a binary assay type

milestones.title: A complex’s binding free energy or an affinity change is predicted within 1 kcal/mol of experiment.
milestones.criterion: A computed binding free energy, ΔG°, or affinity change, ΔΔG, differs from experiment by ≤1 kcal/mol under specified conditions. Relative results establish affinity changes only. For one M2 ligand transformation, Ioannidis et al. in 2016 reported ΔΔGcalc = 0.68 ± 0.21 and ΔΔGexp = 0.35 ± 0.18 kcal/mol. GEMS reported RMSE 1.308 pK units on 285 complexes on 21 October 2025, a different test. For one protein–protein complex, Ras–Raf, Gohlke and Case in 2004 reported −8.3 versus −9.6 kcal/mol, outside this bar.
milestones.set_by: Computational chemistry’s chemical-accuracy convention; applied to small-molecule binding by Ioannidis et al. and discussed for protein–protein binding by Gohlke and Case.
milestones.threshold_quote: Chemical accuracy of 1 kcal mol−1 is considered to be the limit for a deviation of computed from experimental values.

milestones.title: One proteome-wide screen jointly passes binding, complex-geometry and absolute-affinity tests.
milestones.criterion: One frozen workflow screens all protein pairs in a named reference proteome and every protein against a declared small-molecule library. Blinded validation includes both partner classes, protein families absent from training, membrane proteins and disordered regions. All tested binding/nonbinding calls match experimentally determined status at stated detection limits; every structurally measured binder passes m1, and every binder with measured equilibrium affinity has absolute binding-free-energy error ≤1 kcal/mol under specified conditions. Eaves and Woldring’s study, published on 23 June 2026, evaluated five pipelines on 285 confirmed binders without nonbinding pairs.
milestones.set_by: Atlas synthesis; searches of CASP/CAPRI, CACHE and HuRI criteria found no published integrated prospective proteome-wide endpoint.

not_found: Only the abstract and references of the evaluation guidelines published on 23 October 2026 were accessible.

results.finding: Ligand heavy-atom RMSD distributions were evaluated for 285 complexes; the text gives no ligand-pose success rate.
results.detail: The distributions are shown in a figure. The supplied text does not state how many poses had pocket-aligned RMSD below 2 Å.

results.finding: Five affinity models evaluated on 285 complexes achieved a model-averaged crystal-input PCC of 0.839.
results.detail: Correlation with experimental affinities does not establish that any individual absolute binding-free-energy error is within 1 kcal/mol.
results.quote:
As expected, performance is highest when models
are evaluated on crystal complexes (model-averaged PCC = 0.839).

results.finding: Five protein–ligand affinity pipelines were evaluated on 285 confirmed binder complexes.
results.detail: The benchmark did not test nonbinding pairs or screen a complete proteome. It also does not establish the required joint per-binder geometry and absolute-affinity accuracy.
results.quote:
A limitation shared
by this study and PLBAP benchmarking more broadly is that all evaluated
complexes are confirmed protein–ligand binders.

results.finding: FlowDock achieved 51% docking success on 308 protein–ligand complexes.
results.detail: Success used RMSD ≤2 Å and PoseBusters validity after energy minimization. The reported inclusive threshold does not establish the criterion’s strict RMSD <2 Å.
results.quote:
Notably, FlowDock achieves a 10% higher docking success rate
than NeuralPLexer without any structural energy minimization
driven by molecular dynamics software (Eastman et al., 2017),
and with energy minimization its docking success rate increases to
51%, outperforming single-sequence AF3

results.finding: FlowDock’s affinity predictions for 363 PDBBind complexes had an RMSE of 1.363.
results.detail: The aggregate RMSE does not establish a per-complex free-energy error of ≤1 kcal/mol under specified conditions; the table does not state its units.

results.finding: GEMS predicted affinities for 285 protein–ligand complexes with RMSE 1.308 pK units.
results.detail: The reported aggregate error is in pK units, not a per-complex binding-free-energy error in kcal/mol. It does not establish that any particular prediction meets the 1 kcal/mol criterion under specified conditions.
results.quote: a prediction r.m.s.e. of 1.308 and a Pearson correlation of 0.803

results.finding: FragFold predicted native-like binding modes for 13 of 15 inhibitory fragment–protein interactions.
results.detail: The study assessed native-like contacts against full-length protein complex structures using its own criteria; it did not report DockQ.
results.quote: Evaluating inhibitory fragments from known protein–protein interaction interfaces, we find 87% are predicted by FragFold to bind in a native-like mode.

results.finding: For six proteins, 23 of 34 predicted binding clusters matched experimentally measured inhibitory peaks.
results.detail: The in vivo inhibition assay provides functional support, but the reported comparison does not establish two experimental supports including a direct or binary binding assay for a predicted interaction.
results.quote: Across full protein sequences, 68% of FragFold-predicted binding peaks match experimentally measured inhibitory peaks.

results.finding: AlphaFold 3 predicted one NIH-12848 analogue–PI5P4Kγ complex with ligand RMSD of 0.37 Å.
results.detail: This is a selected example, not a benchmark success rate. The paper defines pocket-aligned ligand RMSD using all ligand heavy atoms after alignment to the experimental structure.

results.finding: SiteAF3 predicted 261 protein–peptide complexes with a median DockQ of 0.92.
results.detail: The median exceeds the per-complex threshold, establishing that at least one prediction met it. Results used the best of 15 sampled structures; receptor coordinates were fixed. For multiple receptor chains, DockQ was averaged across chains.

results.detail: Direct binding was measured by SPR, and solubility and aggregation were checked. An orthogonal binding assay was used for fluorinated molecules, but the supplied text does not establish which predicted hits it confirmed or whether those hits passed the checks.
